title: What Happens to Your Online Accounts When You Die, and How to Plan
html:
For a Google account, the one thing you can do today is set up Inactive Account Manager. You choose how long Google should wait, who it should tell, and what they can have. Without a plan, Google says it may delete an account that has been inactive across Google for at least two years. For your other accounts, make a list and tell one person where it is.

Last updated: 10 Oct 2026. This is not legal advice. Talk to a lawyer about a will.

On 11 Oct 2026 I opened my own Google Account's Data and privacy page on my vivo V23 Pro and tapped "Make a plan for your digital legacy". The page is called Your digital legacy. It has Who will download your data ("Allow up to 10 people to download a copy of your data", with an Add data recipient button), Delete your Google Account (Off on mine), When this will happen (mine showed "After 3 months of inactivity") and Settings ("Set reminders, update your contact information, and more"). I only looked at it and did not add anyone.

Google: set up Inactive Account Manager

Go to myaccount.google.com/inactive. Google describes it as a way to share parts of your account data, or tell someone, if you have been inactive for a time you choose. You set how long Google waits. You can name up to 10 people to receive data and choose all of it or only some types of data. Your trusted contacts are notified only after the inactive period has passed.

If you set no plan, Google reserves the right to delete an inactive Google account and its data if you are inactive across Google for at least two years.

What Google says about a person who has died

Google says it can work with immediate family members and representatives to close the account of a person who has died, and in some cases may provide content from the account, after careful review. It says it cannot provide passwords or other login details. It also warns that if you ask for the account to be closed, Google cannot later turn over the contents of the account.

So the plan you make while you are alive matters: families cannot sign in as you, and Google decides requests case by case.

Other accounts

Each service has its own rules. Check the help pages of the apps that hold your photos, chats and money, then note down what each one offers.

In the Instagram app on my vivo V23 Pro there is a Memorialization screen. It says: "Select the profile you want to manage your memorialization preferences for. Memorialization is only available for Instagram and Facebook at this time." My Instagram profile showed "Preference not selected". I did not change it. I read these screens in the app on 11 Oct 2026, not Instagram's help pages.

A simple plan

  1. List your important accounts: email, phone number, bank and UPI, cloud photos, and social accounts. Do not write passwords in the list.
  2. Choose one trusted person and tell them where the list is.
  3. Keep the keys to your email and phone number safe, because they unlock password resets for almost everything else. Use a password manager and keep its recovery details up to date: password managers for Android.
  4. Keep your recovery details current. See the Google account checklist.
  5. Review it once a year.

What to do next

  1. Set up Inactive Account Manager.
  2. Write the list of accounts and tell one person where it is.
  3. Check what your bank and phone operator offer for next of kin, and note it.
